hook: The Suez Canal erased about 7,000km from the Europe–India route.
detail: Opened in 1869, it let ships skip sailing around Africa entirely, reshaping global trade almost overnight.

hook: The Hanseatic League ran Northern European trade for 300 years without being a country.
detail: This medieval network of merchant guilds coordinated trade across the Baltic and North Sea from the 1200s to the 1500s, with no king or capital of its own.

hook: Only fizzy wine from one French region can legally be called Champagne.
detail: The name has been protected since a 1919 treaty. The same method used anywhere else is simply sparkling wine.

hook: William the Conqueror ordered Europe's first great tax survey.
detail: The 1086 Domesday Book catalogued nearly every landholding in England, mainly so the crown could work out how much it could tax.

hook: The Silk Road was never a single road.
detail: It was a shifting web of routes linking China to the Mediterranean, carrying silk, glass and spices alongside ideas like papermaking.

hook: Venice's Rialto market pioneered spreading risk across investors.
detail: Merchants there developed some of Europe earliest marine insurance, splitting the risk of a cargo across several backers instead of one.

hook: Your salary might be named after salt.
detail: The Latin salarium is often linked to salt, a commodity once valuable enough that it may have featured in how Roman soldiers were paid. The link is debated.

hook: The world's first formal stock exchange opened in 1602.
detail: The Amsterdam exchange let investors buy and sell shares in the Dutch East India Company, the first company to issue tradable stock.

hook: Bordeaux was English for three centuries.
detail: From 1152 to 1453 Aquitaine was held by the English crown, which is why claret became the default wine of the English table.

hook: The word ledger comes from a book too heavy to move.
detail: Medieval account books stayed permanently in one place in the church or counting house, from a Middle Dutch word meaning to lie or remain.

hook: The French Revolution gave the world the metre.
detail: In 1791 France defined the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole. The aim was to replace the chaotic patchwork of local units with a single system rooted in nature rather than the body of any particular king.

hook: Lloyd's of London began as a coffee shop where sailors gossiped.
detail: In the 1680s, Edward Lloyd's coffee house near the Thames became the gathering point for merchants, ship captains and underwriters. By 1688 it was the informal centre of the marine insurance market — a function it formalised over the following century.

hook: The pound sterling may be named after a small Norman coin.
detail: One theory traces 'sterling' to the esterlin, a Norman penny introduced after 1066. Another links it to an Old English word for 'little star'. The exact origin is genuinely disputed among etymologists.

hook: Central banks usually target 2% inflation, not 0%.
detail: A little inflation leaves room to cut interest rates before hitting zero, and it stops people delaying purchases while they wait for prices to fall further.

hook: TTF isn't a place — it's a paper hub.
detail: Europe's gas benchmark, the Title Transfer Facility, is a virtual point on the Dutch grid where ownership of gas changes hands, not a physical terminal.

hook: LNG shrinks gas about 600 times over.
detail: Cooling natural gas to around −162°C turns it liquid, shrinking its volume roughly 600-fold so it can travel by tanker instead of pipe.

hook: An inverted yield curve has preceded almost every US recession since the 1950s.
detail: When short-term bonds pay more than long-term ones, it usually signals investors expect the central bank to cut rates as growth slows.

hook: A refiner's real profit is the crack spread.
detail: It is the gap between what a refiner pays for crude oil and what it earns selling the fuels cracked out of it: petrol, diesel, jet fuel.

hook: Backwardation usually means the market is nervous about supply right now.
detail: When futures prices sit below the spot price, traders are pricing in tighter supply today than later. Contango is the mirror image.

hook: One pipeline network from Norway feeds much of Europe.
detail: The Norwegian Continental Shelf links to the UK and mainland Europe through more than 8,000km of subsea pipe, run by the state operator Gassco.

hook: The Big Mac Index is a real economic tool, sort of.
detail: It compares burger prices across countries to test purchasing power parity: the idea that exchange rates should equalise the cost of an identical basket of goods.

hook: Europe races to fill gas storage before winter.
detail: The EU has aimed for storage to sit around 90% full ahead of the heating season, so a cold snap does not collide with tight supply. Live levels are published daily.

hook: Quantitative easing does not involve printing cash.
detail: A central bank creates electronic reserves and uses them to buy bonds, pushing new money into the financial system without a single note printed.

hook: Gas is priced per unit of heat, not volume.
detail: Europe trades in euros per megawatt-hour and the US in dollars per million British thermal units, because what a buyer actually wants is the energy, not the cubic metres.

hook: A cargo can change owner a dozen times mid-ocean.
detail: LNG cargoes are traded as paper title while the ship is still sailing, with the final destination sometimes only fixed days before arrival.

hook: When Asian spot prices beat European ones, LNG cargoes divert mid-voyage.
detail: The JKM–TTF spread is the signal traders watch: if Asian gas is priced high enough above Europe's TTF to cover the extra voyage, cargoes that were sailing for Europe turn around. This arbitrage is what makes LNG a global market rather than a regional one.

hook: A power plant's profit margin has its own name: the spark spread.
detail: It is the difference between the electricity price and the cost of the gas burned to generate it. A dark spread is the same calculation for coal. When either spread goes negative, the plant is losing money every hour it runs.

hook: Norway times its gas field maintenance to summer, not winter.
detail: Planned outages on the Norwegian Continental Shelf are clustered in the months when European demand is lowest and storage is filling. Unexpected winter outages are a different matter — they are the ones that move prices sharply.

hook: Every tonne of CO₂ from a European power plant has a price tag.
detail: The EU Emissions Trading System requires large emitters to hold one permit for each tonne of CO₂ they release. Permits are auctioned and traded; when their price rises, coal-fired generation becomes more expensive relative to gas, shifting the dispatch order.

hook: An LNG terminal's send-out rate is rarely the same as its nameplate capacity.
detail: Regasification capacity is the maximum rate a terminal can vaporise LNG and push it into the grid. Actual send-out depends on downstream demand and shipper nominations, so terminals routinely run well below their stated maximum.

hook: TTF became Europe's gas benchmark partly because of Dutch grid rules.
detail: The Netherlands operates an entry–exit system that lets any shipper trade at the virtual hub without needing a specific delivery point. That flexibility drove liquidity towards TTF and away from older hubs like the UK's NBP.

hook: Which country holds the world's largest proven natural gas reserves?
detail: Russia, with Iran and Qatar close behind. Together the top three hold well over half the world proven reserves.

hook: What does backwardation mean in a futures market?
detail: Futures prices sitting below the spot price, usually a sign traders see supply as tighter right now than later.

hook: Roughly what share of EU gas demand did Russian pipeline gas meet before 2022?
detail: Around 40%, a share that collapsed after the invasion of Ukraine as the EU raced to diversify supply.

hook: What is the name of Norway's state gas transport operator?
detail: Gassco, which runs the integrated pipeline system carrying gas from the Norwegian Continental Shelf to Europe.

hook: What is the rough shrinkage factor when gas is turned into LNG?
detail: About 600 times, which is exactly why it is economic to ship gas across oceans instead of piping it.

hook: What does the acronym TTF stand for?
detail: Title Transfer Facility, the Dutch virtual trading point that serves as the European gas benchmark.

hook: What decade did the Amsterdam stock exchange open?
detail: The 1600s, in 1602, founded by the Dutch East India Company.

hook: What treaty first gave legal protection to the name Champagne?
detail: The Treaty of Versailles, 1919.

hook: What 1086 document is one of Europe's earliest large-scale property surveys?
detail: The Domesday Book, commissioned by William the Conqueror.

hook: Which sea did the Hanseatic League mainly trade across?
detail: The Baltic, alongside the North Sea, linking towns from Novgorod to Bruges.

hook: What does the benchmark JKM measure in energy markets?
detail: The Japan-Korea Marker — the spot reference price for LNG delivered to northeast Asia. Alongside TTF in Europe and Henry Hub in the US, it is one of the three main regional gas price benchmarks.

hook: Which commodity was first traded on a formal futures exchange?
detail: Grain — specifically wheat and corn, on the Chicago Board of Trade, founded in 1848. Futures let farmers lock in a price before harvest, reducing the ruinous price swings that followed a glut.

hook: What does the French label AOC guarantee on a bottle of wine?
detail: That the wine was made in a specific named region using approved grape varieties and methods. AOC (appellation d'origine contrôlée) is France's geographically-tied quality classification — the model that inspired the EU's PDO system used for food and drink across Europe.
